stories.title: 5.9-magnitude earthquake strikes eastern Japan, strong jolt felt in Tokyo
stories.summary: A 5.9-magnitude earthquake struck eastern Japan on Aug 23, with a strong jolt felt in Tokyo and surrounding prefectures, causing injuries and some infrastructure damage. No tsunami threat or abnormalities were reported at nearby nuclear power plants, including Fukushima and Tokai No. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi ordered damage assessments and timely public updates, while the Japan Meteorological Agency warned of possible aftershocks over the next week. An earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 5.9 struck eastern Japan early on Aug 23, with a strong jolt felt in the capital Tokyo, but it posed no threat of tsunami, the weather agency said. The 2am (1am Singapore time) quake originated in the southern part of Ibaraki prefecture at a depth of 68km, registering lower 5 on the Japanese seismic intensity scale in parts of the prefecture as well as in central Tokyo. Multiple people were injured in the earthquake, including a young man and a woman in her 70s in Saitama, near Tokyo, as well as three people in Kawasaki, just south of Tokyo, according to local fire departments. In Tokyo’s Koto ward, a water main ruptured, prompting metropolitan authorities to look into whether the damage was linked to the quake. A lower-5 intensity was also recorded in parts of Saitama and Chiba prefectures. In central Tokyo, the same intensity was registered in Adachi ward, while other parts of the capital recorded lower intensities. No abnormalities were detected at the Tokai No. 2 nuclear power plant in Ibaraki prefecture, according to its operator. No abnormalities were also reported at the disaster-struck Fukushima Daiichi plant and the nearby Fukushima Daini nuclear power plant, both north of the prefecture, according to their operator.

stories.title: Tropical Storm Moke advances towards Hawaii with heavy rain, strong winds
stories.summary: For the second week in a row, Hawaii Island, also known as the Big Island, faces threats from an intensifying storm. Tropical Storm Moke is grinding towards Hawaii, bringing gusts of wind and heavy rain only a week after the islands faced similar conditions from Hurricane Lala. On Saturday, Hawaii residents prepared for the latest storm, which is expected to pass south of Hawaii Island, the largest island in the Hawaiian archipelago, overnight and into the following morning. As of 11am Hawaii Standard Time (21:00 GMT), Moke was located about 684 kilometres, or 425 miles, south of Hilo, a city on the eastern coast of Hawaii Island. It was moving west-northwest at 19km/h (12mph). The National Hurricane Center (NHC) in the United States reported that the storm’s maximum sustained winds were about 85km/h (50mph). Moke, like Lala, is forecast to spare the Big Island a potentially disastrous direct hit. But the island is still recovering from Lala, a Category 1 storm that spurred heavy flooding and power outages. At least one person died in last weekend’s storm. Lala came close enough to Hawaii Island to dump more than 1,000mm (39 inches) of rain in some locations, causing rivers to burst their banks. High winds also bent tall palm trees and downed electrical lines, forcing nearly 130,000 utility customers to lose power. Hawaii Governor Josh Green and other state officials have urged people to prepare for Moke by restocking food, medicine and other daily essentials ahead of the storm’s passage.
